newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, palladium prices soar on supply fears.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, palladium prices soar on supply fears.

text.p: Coffee futures soared to a 20-year high on Wednesday amid growing concern about a shortage of high quality arabica beans, while supply fears drove palladium prices to a 17-year peak, traders said.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery closed 21.25 cents a pound higher at 295.55 cents, just below a 20-year high of 297.00 cents reached earlier in the day.
"This market is like a freight train -- don't get in front of it," said Victor Henriquez, president of Miami-based Hencorp-Becstone. "No one wants to be short."

Coffee prices headed higher at the outset, defying pre-opening expectations, as speculators followed through on Tuesday's buying spree. Traders said weather forecasts calling for below normal temperatures later this week in top producer Brazil also prompted buying.

Although weather forecasters said temperatures in Brazil's coffee belt are not expected to drop low enough to cause damage to coffee trees, traders said any signs of cool weather at a time when inventories in consuming and producing countries hover near 20-year lows will spark panic buying.
Two severe frosts in 1994, in June and July, damaged more than half of Brazil's coffee trees and sent world prices reeling higher.
"There was no change or nothing new," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "The fundamentals are the same. They just become more bullish because of the coming winter in Brazil.
The two-day speculative buying frenzy has driven the July contract up 38.70 cents, or 15 percent, since Friday's close.

Forecasts for smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries, labor unrest in Colombia and Brazil and projections for a smaller crop in Brazil in the coming 1997/98 season have heightened supply worries.

But as prices continue to climb, roasters have been forced to pass higher costs to consumers. Some operators fear some coffee drinkers may soon shun the higher-priced brew and opt for other beverages.
On Wednesday, Starbucks Corp. said it planned to raise prices for the second time on its coffee prices to reflect the higher cost of coffee beans worldwide.
The Seattle-based retailer and roaster said most coffee beverage prices will increase by $0.05 to $0.10 a cup, while the price of whole beans will increase by $0.40 a pound, effective on Friday.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, palladium prices soared to a 17-year high as the market's nerve finally snapped on news of a strike in South Africa amid tight physical supplies.
Palladium for June delivery settled $28.15 higher at $202.65 an ounce, just off the day's high of $204.00.

The run-up in palladium and platinum, the latter back to February's highs, followed news of a wildcat strike at Anglo American Platinum Corp. Ltd.'s (Amplats) Rustenburg platinum mine in South Africa, the world's biggest.
"It was the straw that broke the camel's back," a dealer said.
White metal supplies were already tight because Russia has not shipped any of its 1997 platinum and palladium exports. The cost to borrow the metal has soared lately.
But after close of New York trading Wednesday, Amplats said the strike was over and employees were returning to work.
NYMEX platinum for July delivery settled $13.50 firmer at $410.50 an ounce, after ranging from $396.50 to $411.00.
Crude oil futures at the NYMEX ended little changed after a slow session, content to rest following Tuesday's steep losses.

Crude oil for July delivery closed unchanged at $20.79 a barrel, with June unleaded gasoline ending 0.42 cent a gallon higher at 65.80 cents and June heating oil ending up 0.12 cent a gallon at 55.39 cents.
Prices had fallen on Tuesday as talk of sufficient supply of both crude oil and unleaded gasoline put an end to the market's recent strength.
